chunks: How a camera works. The question: How does a camera work?
A camera is a lens that projects a picture of the scene onto a chip covered in a grid of tiny light meters.
Each light meter, called a pixel, collects light for a short time and turns it into a number. Put all the numbers together and you have the image.
Hold a magnifying glass near a sheet of paper and a small, sharp picture of the window appears on it.
Now replace the paper with a grid of millions of tiny light meters, each reading one dot of that picture. The lens decides where each bit of the scene lands.
The picture breaks down in one way: the meters cannot tell colors apart, so each one gets a tiny red, green or blue filter, and the missing colors are guessed afterward.
Focusing from infinity to 10 cm takes only about a third of a millimeter of motion, which is why a small voice-coil motor (VCM) is enough.
Most of the travel is used up for close subjects, and the depth of field is huge at long distances because of the small sensor and short focal length.
Pixel: one light meter on the chip. It turns light into electrons, tiny packets of electric charge.
Exposure: the time the pixel spends collecting light, together with how wide the lens opening is.
Color filter array (Bayer): a mosaic of red, green and blue filters, one per pixel. ADC: a circuit that turns a voltage into a number.
Image signal processor (ISP): the chip block that turns raw numbers into a finished picture.
Say 400 photons land on one pixel during the exposure, and 60 percent of them free an electron. The pixel collects 240 electrons. The ADC turns that into a number.
Light arrives randomly, so the count wobbles by about its square root: about 15 electrons. Now dim the scene to a quarter of the light.
The pixel gets 60 electrons, with noise of about 8. The signal fell four times, but the noise only halved, so the dim image looks grainier.
"A camera focuses the scene with a lens onto a sensor made of millions of photodiodes. Each pixel converts photons to electrons during the exposure, under a Bayer color filter.
The charge is converted to a voltage, amplified, which is the ISO gain, and digitized by an ADC into a raw mosaic.

An image signal processor then demosaics, white-balances, denoises, tone-maps and compresses it, while an autofocus, auto-exposure and white-balance loop controls the lens, exposure time and gain for the next frame."
